business.title: Tempered fractional GMV self-tuning control of PV-fed boost converters with causal prediction and closed-loop stability analysis
business.description: Regulating the DC-link voltage of a boost converter fed by a photovoltaic (PV) source is complicated by stochastic irradiance, fluctuating loads, and drifting component characteristics. Fractional-order descriptions can encode the memory that such hardware exhibits, yet the power-law kernel of a conventional fractional operator weighs the distant past too heavily: adaptation slows under nonstationary operation, and the resulting regressors become long and numerically ill-conditioned, which degrades on-line identification. Here we attenuate that kernel exponentially—a tempering that yields semi-long memory—and build around it a complete adaptive scheme, the tempered–fractional generalized minimum-variance self-tuning regulator (TF–GMV–STR). The development proceeds in four steps. (i) An operating-point linearization links the fractional averaged converter model to a discrete model class; within this class, a one-step predictor in innovation (ARMAX-type) form is constructed from a truncated tempered Grünwald–Letnikov basis and rendered strictly causal by an explicit monic normalization, repairing an algebraic flaw common to naive fractional predictors. (ii) Minimizing the quadratic GMV cost—rather than postulating the controller structure—produces an offset-free incremental control law in which the $$\rho /\hat{b}_1$$ weighting of the controller polynomial emerges from the optimality condition itself; a finite tempered Diophantine identity and a recursive extended least-squares estimator with projection complete the loop. (iii) The closed-loop characteristic polynomial is proved to admit the factorization $$\widetilde{C}\,[\,q\widetilde{B}+(\rho /\hat{b}_1)A_\Delta \,]$$, so stability reduces to a verifiable frozen-time (small-signal) Schur test, verified here uniformly over the entire admissible parameter set of the reported configuration (worst-case root modulus 0.54); a conditional boundedness proposition and the leading-coefficient bound $$z_0=\hat{b}_1+\rho /\hat{b}_1\ge 2\sqrt{\rho }$$ follow, while large-signal operation is probed numerically through a full-range start-up and disturbance transients on the nonlinear averaged converter. (iv) Performance is assessed against two baselines—an integer-order GMV–STR and an untempered long-memory fractional GMV–STR—using common random numbers and paired hypothesis tests across 40 realizations, spanning fixed-reference regulation, set-point steps, load/source disturbances, a deliberate memory-mismatch experiment, and closed-loop operation on the nonlinear averaged fractional converter. In regulation, the proposed scheme is statistically indistinguishable from the long-memory fractional baseline ($$p\ge 0.69$$) and ahead of the integer one in ISE only (paired $$p=0.042$$, a small effect, Cohen’s $$d=0.33$$). The unambiguous gains are realization-side and orthogonal to regulation quality: the tempered scheme runs on 2–$$4.5\times $$ fewer memory taps and carries a $$\sim \!38\%$$ lower information-matrix condition number—properties well matched to embedded power-electronic targets.

business.title: Helicobacter pylori infection, hyperuricemia, and serum uric acid levels: The role of metabolic, renal, and inflammatory factors in a large health examination population
business.description: Background Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection has been linked to several extragastric metabolic disorders. However, its cross-sectional association with hyperuricemia remains uncertain, partly because previous studies have often been limited by small sample sizes and incomplete adjustment for metabolic and renal factors. Methods This large-scale cross-sectional study used data from a health examination database. The main regression analyses included 67,826 participants with valid H. pylori status, serum uric acid measurements, hyperuricemia classification, age, sex, and BMI. Modified Poisson regression with a log link and HC0 robust sandwich variance was used to estimate prevalence ratios for hyperuricemia, while linear regression with HC3 heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors was used for continuous serum uric acid. Sex-stratified and robustness analyses were also performed. Results In the unadjusted model, H. pylori infection was associated with higher prevalence of hyperuricemia (PR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.22–1.32, p < 0.001). This association was progressively attenuated after sequential adjustment and was small in the extended clinical model (PR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.98–1.06, p = 0.269). For continuous serum uric acid, H. pylori positivity remained associated with a small increase after full adjustment (β = 2.14 μmol/L, 95% CI: 0.80–3.49, p = 0.002). Functional-form sensitivity analyses yielded similarly small effect estimates for hyperuricemia, although statistical significance varied across model specifications. Sex-stratified and robustness analyses were generally consistent with these findings. Conclusion In this large health examination population, any remaining association between H. pylori positivity and hyperuricemia after comprehensive adjustment was small and sensitive to model specification. H. pylori positivity was also associated with a statistically detectable but clinically modest difference in continuous serum uric acid levels. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should not be interpreted causally.

science.title: Structural basis of condensate formation of VAPB protein
science.description: Vesicle-associated membrane protein-associated protein B (VAPB) is an endoplasmic reticulum protein implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) through its P56S mutation. Although pathological function loss and condensate formation of the VAPB P56S mutant are crucial for disease progression, the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we investigated the structural basis of VAPB condensate formation using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, turbidity analysis, and microscopy. Our results show that the major sperm protein domain of VAPB undergoes temperature-dependent condensate formation, a process regulated by localized structural dynamics. We identified a pH-sensitive hydrogen bond that functions as a switch to autoinhibition of condensate formation, as well as a flexible loop whose slow dynamics facilitate the multivalent interactions essential for condensate formation. The ALS-linked P56S mutant exhibits markedly enhanced condensate formation, which is associated with increased conformational heterogeneity that may promote aberrant intermolecular contacts related to pathological function loss. These findings reveal how specific dynamic features within a folded protein can drive condensate formation, providing a molecular framework for understanding both VAPB function and its pathological condensate formation.
